NOVELTY STATEMENT
Standard practice tracks brush temperature and vibration as direct indicators of mechanical wear. My observable is the electrical contact resistance inferred from the excitation current ripple pattern at the 1-minute sampling interval, which captures the progressive micro-arcing and intermittent contact loss that precedes complete failure by weeks. This departure connects to failure physics through the stochastic nature of electrical contact degradation: as brush wear increases, the contact area decreases, causing higher resistance and more pronounced current fluctuations that standard RMS current measurements would miss.

PHYSICS CHECK
The governing physical relation is Ohm's Law (V = IR) combined with the statistical distribution of contact resistance fluctuations. For a healthy contact, resistance follows a narrow Gaussian distribution. As wear progresses, the distribution broadens and develops a tail representing intermittent high-resistance states. A magnitude verification: a healthy brush might show a resistance standard deviation of 0.1% of nominal, while approaching failure this could increase to 5% or more. This 50-fold increase is detectable even with 1-minute sampling given the excitation system's current magnitude (typically hundreds of amps).

IMPLEMENTATION BILL
Components: Existing plant historian with 1-minute sampling of excitation current and voltage; standard engineering workstation with Python/R capabilities; statistical analysis software (open-source or off-the-shelf).
Materials: None needed beyond existing data infrastructure.
Instruments: No new hardware required.
Procedure: 
1. Calculate instantaneous resistance from V and I measurements at each sample point
2. Compute rolling 24-hour standard deviation of resistance values
3. Apply exponential smoothing to the standard deviation values to reduce noise
4. Compare smoothed value against threshold
All computation uses standard statistical functions available in common engineering software packages.

- Installability: SAME - no new hardware installation required

The approach imposes no additional deployment burden compared to standard temperature/vibration monitoring while providing earlier detection of the specific failure mode.

EXECUTABLE TEST
Protocol: 
1. Collect historical data from at least 5 generators with known brush wear histories (2 healthy, 3 with documented wear progression)
2. Apply the algorithm to each dataset
3. Record detection time relative to actual maintenance date
Instruments: Existing historian data; standard engineering workstation
Pass/Fail Threshold: Must detect all 3 wear cases at least 14 days before maintenance with no false positives in the 2 healthy cases
Duration: 1 week for data processing and analysis
Kill Criterion: If any wear case is detected less than 14 days before maintenance OR if any false positive occurs in healthy cases, the predictor is invalidated.
